clinicalPearls: A benign paroxysmal disorder of the superior oblique muscle causing brief episodes of monocular oscillopsia and torsional-vertical diplopia
Attacks are typically short, frequent and precipitated by looking in the direction of the affected superior oblique
The high-frequency low-amplitude movements may be hard to see and are best appreciated on slit-lamp or fundus examination
It is usually idiopathic but has been attributed to neurovascular compression of the trochlear nerve
Most cases are benign, though MRI is warranted to exclude a posterior fossa lesion
Membrane-stabilising drugs or, in refractory cases, surgery or microvascular decompression may be considered
reference.pathophysiology: Superior oblique myokymia is thought to arise from ephaptic transmission or aberrant regeneration within the trochlear nerve, in some cases related to vascular compression at the nerve root exit, producing spontaneous high-frequency contraction of the superior oblique muscle. The resulting small torsional and vertical eye movements are perceived as shimmering monocular oscillopsia and transient diplopia.
additionalDifferentials: Trochlear nerve palsy with aberrant regeneration
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp or fundus observation of the fine torsional movements
MRI of the brain and orbits to exclude posterior fossa or trochlear-nerve lesions
Orthoptic assessment of ocular alignment and motility
Video-oculography where available to characterise the movements
redFlags: Associated other cranial neuropathies suggesting a structural lesion
Onset after head trauma with additional deficits
reference.prognosis: The disorder is benign and may remit spontaneously or respond to medical therapy; symptoms can be intrusive but do not threaten sight.
pitfalls: Overlooking the subtle movements and labelling symptoms functional
Omitting MRI and missing a compressive posterior fossa lesion
Confusing it with ocular neuromyotonia, which causes sustained rather than shimmering deviation
Assuming persistent diplopia rather than the characteristic paroxysms
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Reassure and observe, as the disorder is benign and may remit spontaneously
Offer membrane-stabilising drugs such as carbamazepine or gabapentin to suppress attacks
Consider a topical or systemic beta-blocker such as timolol or propranolol as an alternative medical option
Arrange MRI of the brain and orbits to exclude a posterior fossa or trochlear-nerve lesion
Reserve strabismus surgery or microvascular decompression for disabling, drug-refractory symptoms
Refer to neuro-ophthalmology for assessment and ongoing management
